title: The names of God and the nature of names
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτά φησιν ὅτι οἱ αἰπόλοι καὶ ποιμένες ἕνα ἐνόμισαν θεὸν, εἴτε ὕψιστον εἴτ᾿ Ἀδωναῒ εἴτ᾿ οὐράνιον εἴτε Σαβαὼθ, εἴτε καὶ ὅπῃ καὶ ὅπως χαίρουσιν ὀνομάζοντες τόνδε τὸν κόσμον· καὶ πλεῖον οὐδὲν ἔγνωσαν. καὶ ἑξῆς δέ φησι μηδὲν διαφέρειν τῷ παρ᾿ Ἕλλησι φερομένῳ ὀνόματι τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν καλεῖν Δία ἢ τῷ δεῖνα, φέρ᾿ εἰπεῖν. παρ᾿ Ἰνδοῖς ἢ τῷ δεῖνα παρ᾿ Αἰγυπτίοις. λεκτέον δὲ καὶ πρὸς τοῦτο ὅτι ἐμπίπτει εἰς τὸ προκείμενον λόγος βαθὺς καὶ ἀπόῤῥητος. ὁ περὶ φύσεως ὀνομάτων· πότερον. ὡς οἴεται Ἀριστοτέλης, θέσει εἰσὶ τὰ ὀνόματα ἢ. ὡς νομίζουσιν οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς, φύσει, μιμουμένων τῶν πρώτων φωνῶν τὰ πράγματα, καθ᾿ ὧν τὰ ὀνόματα, καθὸ καὶ στοιχεῖά τινα (τῆς) ἐτυμολογίας εἰσάγουσιν, ἢ, ὡς διδάσκει Ἐπίκουρος, ἑτἐρως ἢ ὡς οἴονται οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς, φύσει ἐστὶ τὰ ὀνόματα, ἀποῤῥηξάντων τῶν πρώτων ἀνθρώπων τινὰς φωνὰς κατὰ τῶν πραγμάτων. ἐὰν τοίνυν δυνηθῶμεν ἐν προηγουμένῳ λόγῳ παραστῆσαι φύσιν ὀνομάτων ἐνεργῶν, ὧν τισι χρῶνται Αἰγυπτίων οἱ σοφοὶ ἢ τῶν παρὰ Πέρσαις μάγων οἱ λόγιοι ἢ τῶν παρ᾿ Ἰνδοῖς φιλοσοφούντων Βραχμᾶνες ἢ Σαμαναῖοι. καὶ οὕτω καθ᾿ ἕκαστον τῶν ἐθνῶν, καὶ κατασκευάσαι οἷοί τε γενώμεθα ὅτι καὶ ἡ καλουμένη μαγεία οὐχ, ὡς οἴονται οἱ ἀπὸ Ἐπικούρου καὶ Ἀριστοτέλους, πρᾶγμά ἐστιν ἀσύστατον πάντῃ ἀλλ᾿, ὡς οἱ περὶ ταῦτα δεινοὶ ἀποδεικνύουσι, συνεστὸς μὲν λόγους δ᾿ ἔχον σφόδρα ὀλίγοις γινωσκομένους· τότ᾿ ἐροῦμεν ὅτι τὸ μὲν Σαβαὼθ ὄνομα καὶ τὸ Ἀδωναῒ καὶ (ὅσα) ἄλλα παρ᾿ Ἑβραίοις μετὰ πολλῆς σεμνολογίας παραδιδόμενα οὐκ ἐπὶ τῶν τυχόντων καὶ γενητῶν κεῖται πραγμάτων ἀλλ᾿ ἐπί τινος θεολογίας ἀποῤῥήτου, ἀναφερομένης εἰς τὸν τῶν ὅλων δημιουργόν. διὸ καὶ δύναται ταῦτα τὰ ὀνόματα. λεγόμενα μετά τινος τοῦ συνυφοῦς αὐτοῖς εἱρμοῦ. ἄλλα δὲ κατὰ Αἰγυπτίαν φερόμενα φωνὴν ἐπί τινων δαιμόνων. τῶν τάδε μόνα δυναμένων, καὶ ἄλλα κατὰ τὴν Περσῶν διάλεκτον ἐπὶ ἄλλων δυνάμεων, καὶ οὕτω καθ᾿ ἕκαστον τῶν ἐθνῶν, εἰς χρείας τινὰς παραλαμβάνεσθαι. καὶ οὕτως εὑρεθήσεται τῶν ἐπὶ γῆς δαιμόνων, λαχόντων διαφόρους τόπους, φέρεσθαι τὰ ὀνόματα οἰκείως ταῖς κατὰ τόπον καὶ ἔθνος διαλέκτοις. ὁ τοίνυν μεγαλοφυέστερον κἂν ὀλίγην τούτων περίνοιαν εἰληφὼς εὐλαβηθήσεται ἄλλα ἄλλοις ἐφαρμόζειν ὀνόματα πράγμασι, μή ποτε ὅμοιον πάθῃ τοῖς τὸ θεὸς ὄνομα ἐσφαλμένως φέρουσιν ἐπὶ ὕλην ἄψυχον. ἢ τὴν τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ προσηγορίαν κατασπῶσιν ἀπὸ τοῦ πρώτου αἰτίου ἢ ἀπὸ τῆς ἀρετῆς καὶ τοῦ καλοῦ ἐπὶ τὸν τυφλὸν πλοῦτον καὶ ἐπὶ τὴν σαρκῶν καὶ αἱμάτων καὶ ὀστέων συμμετρίαν ἐν ὑγείᾳ καὶ εὐεξίᾳ ἢ τὴν νομιζομένην εὐγένειαν.
pass_a_gloss: After these he says that the goatherds and shepherds thought (νομίζω) one God, whether Most High (ὕψιστος) or Adonai or Heavenly (οὐράνιος) or Sabaoth, or also wherever and however they delight (χαίρω) naming (ὀνομάζω) this world (κόσμος); and they knew (γιγνώσκω) nothing more. And next he says it differs (διαφέρω) nothing to call (καλέω) the God over all (ὁ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεός) by the name current (φέρω) among Greeks, Zeus, or by such-and-such (ὁ δεῖνα), say, among Indians, or such-and-such among Egyptians. It must be said also to this that there falls into (ἐμπίπτω) the matter before us (τὸ προκείμενον) a deep and secret (ἀπόρρητος) account/inquiry (λόγος), the one about the nature (φύσις) of names: whether, as Aristotle thinks, names are by imposition/convention (θέσει) or, as those from the Stoa think, by nature (φύσει), the first sounds (φωναί) imitating (μιμέομαι) the things (πράγματα) of which the names [are], according to which they also introduce certain elements (στοιχεῖα) of etymology (ἐτυμολογία); or, as Epicurus teaches, otherwise (ἑτέρως) than the Stoics think, names are by nature, the first men having burst out (ἀπορρήγνυμι) certain sounds concerning (κατά + gen.) things. If then we can, in a principal/dedicated discussion (ἐν προηγουμένῳ λόγῳ), establish (παρίστημι) the nature of effective names (ὀνόματα ἐνεργά), some of which the wise of the Egyptians use, or the learned (λόγιοι) of the magi (μάγοι) among Persians, or of those philosophising among Indians the Brahmans or Samanaeans, and so in each of the nations; and become able to prove (κατασκευάζω) that also so-called magic (μαγεία) is not, as those from Epicurus and Aristotle think, a thing wholly without coherence/substance (ἀσύστατον), but, as those skilled (δεινοί) about these demonstrate (ἀποδείκνυμι), consistent/real (συνεστός) yet having principles (λόγοι) known to very few; then we will say that the name Sabaoth and Adonai and (whatever) others handed down (παραδίδωμι) among Hebrews with much solemnity (σεμνολογία) lie (κεῖμαι) not upon ordinary (τυχόντα) and generated (γενητά) things but upon a certain secret theology (θεολογία ἀπόρρητος) referred (ἀναφέρω) to the craftsman of the universe (ὁ τῶν ὅλων δημιουργός). Wherefore these names also can (δύναται), spoken with a certain sequence (εἱρμός) woven together (συνυφής) with them, and others current in Egyptian speech upon certain demons (δαίμονες) able [to do] only these things, and others in the dialect of Persians upon other powers (δυνάμεις), and so in each of the nations, be taken up (παραλαμβάνω) for certain uses (χρεῖαι). And thus it will be found that the names of the demons on earth, who obtained by lot (λαγχάνω) different places (τόποι), are borne appropriately (οἰκείως) to the dialects by place and nation. He then who has taken, in a more high-minded way (μεγαλοφυέστερον), even a little insight (περίνοια) of these will beware (εὐλαβέομαι) of fitting (ἐφαρμόζω) different names to different things, lest he suffer (πάσχω) like those who wrongly (ἐσφαλμένως) carry the name 'God' onto lifeless matter (ὕλη ἄψυχος), or drag down (κατασπάω) the appellation (προσηγορία) of the good (τὸ ἀγαθόν) from the first cause (τὸ πρῶτον αἴτιον) or from virtue (ἀρετή) and the beautiful (τὸ καλόν) onto blind wealth (τυφλὸς πλοῦτος) and onto the symmetry/proportion (συμμετρία) of fleshes and bloods and bones in health (ὑγεία) and good condition (εὐεξία), or the supposed noble birth (εὐγένεια).
pass_b_english: After this he says that "the goatherds and shepherds thought there was one God, whether Most High, or Adonai, or the Heavenly One, or Sabaoth, or however and in whatever way they like to name this world; and they knew nothing more." And next he says that "it makes no difference whether one calls the God over all by the name current among the Greeks, Zeus, or by such-and-such a name, say, among the Indians, or by such-and-such among the Egyptians."

To this too we must reply that the present subject involves a deep and secret question: the question of the nature of names. Are names a matter of convention, as Aristotle thinks (Aristotle, On Interpretation 2)? Or are they by nature, as the Stoics hold, the first sounds imitating the things the names stand for, which is why the Stoics also bring in certain elements of etymology? Or are names by nature, as Epicurus teaches, though in a different way from what the Stoics think, because the first men burst out with certain sounds in response to things (Epicurus, Letter to Herodotus 75–76)?

Suppose, then, that in a treatment devoted to the subject we can establish the nature of names that have power, some of which are used by the wise among the Egyptians, or the learned among the Persian magi, or, among the philosophers of India, by the Brahmans or the Samanaeans, and so on in each of the nations. And suppose we can also prove that what is called magic is not, as the followers of Epicurus and Aristotle think, a thing wholly without coherence, but, as those skilled in it demonstrate, a coherent system, though its principles are known to very few. Then we shall say that the name Sabaoth, and Adonai, and the other names handed down among the Hebrews with great reverence, are not applied to ordinary, created things, but belong to a certain secret theology which refers to the Maker of the universe. This is why these names, when they are spoken with a certain sequence that is woven into them, can be employed for certain purposes; and so can others, current in the Egyptian tongue and applied to certain demons who can do only these particular things, and others, in the Persian language, applied to other powers; and so in each of the nations. And so it will be found that the names of the demons on earth, who have been allotted different places, are spoken in a way suited to the language of each place and nation.

Whoever, then, has with a nobler mind gained even a little insight into these matters will take care not to fit names to things that are not theirs. Otherwise he may suffer the same as those who wrongly apply the name "God" to lifeless matter, or who drag down the title "good" from the First Cause, or from virtue and the beautiful, to blind wealth, to the right proportion of flesh, blood and bones in health and good condition, or to what is counted noble birth.

choices.choice: Both Celsus sentences are reported (ὅτι ... ; φησι + infinitive) but keep his wording, so they are in quotation marks. Celsus's list: ὕψιστος ('Most High'), Ἀδωναΐ, οὐράνιος ('Heavenly One'), Σαβαώθ; these are divine titles found in the Greek Bible but Celsus is listing names, not quoting, so no inline citation. 'Name this world': Celsus implies the Jews' God is just the cosmos. Read ἑτέρως for the TEI's ἑτἐρως. The Epicurus clause (ἑτέρως ἢ ὡς οἴονται οἱ ἀπὸ τῆς Στοᾶς) is taken as 'by nature, but otherwise than the Stoics think'. Aristotle's view of names as by convention (κατὰ συνθήκην) is On Interpretation 2 (16a19–29); Epicurus on the natural origin of names is Letter to Herodotus 75–76; both cited inline as the doctrines Origen names, not as quotations. ἐν προηγουμένῳ λόγῳ = 'in a treatment devoted to the subject'. The infinitive παραλαμβάνεσθαι is construed with δύναται ('can be employed'), with ἄλλα δὲ ... and ἄλλα ... depending on the same verb. Samanaeans (Σαμαναῖοι) = Indian ascetics (śramaṇas), kept as Origen's name. ἄλλα ἄλλοις ἐφαρμόζειν ὀνόματα πράγμασι ('fit different names to different things') rendered 'fit names to things that are not theirs', the sense required by ch. 25's 'interchanges the names'. 'Blind wealth' is a stock phrase (cf. Plato, Laws 631c, which says wealth that is not blind); not cited.
'falls under the present subject' (calque of ἐμπίπτει εἰς τὸ προκείμενον) -> 'the present subject involves'
Epicurus clause: 'sounds about things' -> 'in response to things' (κατὰ τῶν πραγμάτων)
ἀσύστατον / συνεστός: 'without substance ... something real' -> 'without coherence ... a coherent system'
removed addition 'of sounds' (εἱρμός is unspecified); made the ἄλλα ... ἄλλα clauses depend on 'can be employed' as in the Greek, 'over' -> 'applied to' (ἐπί + gen.)
Aristotle On Interpretation 2 and Epicurus Letter to Herodotus 75-76 checked as the doctrines named
